title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
directAnswer: Find the kth largest value (kth in sorted-descending order), not the kth distinct value. The interview-standard answer is a min-heap of size k: scan the array, keep only the k largest seen, and the heap's root is the answer — O(n log k) time, O(k) space. If asked to beat that, quickselect partitions around a random pivot to find the (n−k)th smallest index in O(n) average time, O(1) extra space.

remember.pattern: Min-heap of size k (selection) / Quickselect partition
remember.formula:
min-heap of size k:
    for x in nums:
        push x
        if len(heap) > k: pop_min()   # evict smallest, keep top k
    return heap.peek()                 # kth largest

quickselect: find index n-k in partition order (kth largest = (n-k)th smallest)
rules: kth **largest** = (n−k)th **smallest** in 0-indexed sorted order — that index is quickselect's target.
The size-k **min-heap** keeps the k largest seen; its root is the *smallest of the largest* = the kth largest.
Min-heap (not max-heap) for kth largest: you evict the **smallest** so only big values survive — heap size never exceeds k → O(n log k).
**Randomize the quickselect pivot** to dodge the O(n²) worst case on sorted/adversarial input.
Quickselect recurses into **only one side** of the partition — that's why it's O(n) average, not O(n log n).
It's kth largest by **value with duplicates counted**, not kth distinct — [3,3,3], k=2 is still 3.
whenToUse: Need the kth largest/smallest (or top-k) and full sorting is overkill
Streaming data where you keep only the k best seen so far → size-k heap
One-shot selection on an in-memory array and you want O(n) average → quickselect
k is much smaller than n (heap shines: O(n log k) ≪ O(n log n))
antiSignals: Need the array fully sorted afterward → just sort, the kth element falls out
Need kth *distinct* value → dedupe first, then select
Strict worst-case O(n) required → median-of-medians, not random quickselect
Many repeated queries for different k → sort once, answer each in O(1)
remember.takeaway: Selecting the kth largest is the canonical 'don't fully sort' problem. A size-k min-heap gives a clean O(n log k) you can code under pressure; quickselect gives O(n) average by partitioning toward one target index. Knowing both — and when each wins — is exactly what the interviewer is probing.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you avoid the trivial full-sort, reach for a heap sized to k (not n), and can articulate quickselect's O(n)-average partition idea — plus the index arithmetic kth largest = (n−k)th smallest.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using a max-heap and popping k times (O(n + k log n), heap of size n) when a size-k min-heap is tighter, or botching the quickselect target index / forgetting to randomize the pivot (O(n²) on sorted input).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Offer the spectrum: sort (O(n log n), simplest), size-k min-heap (O(n log k), great for streaming/small k), quickselect (O(n) average, in-place). State the trade-offs and pick based on constraints.

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return *the* `kᵗʰ` *largest element in the array*.

Note that it is the `kᵗʰ` largest element in the **sorted order**, not the `kᵗʰ` distinct element.

Can you solve it without sorting?
understanding: Return the value that would sit at position k from the largest end if the array were sorted descending. Duplicates count toward the rank — it is not the kth distinct value. k is guaranteed valid (1 ≤ k ≤ n).

clarifyingQuestions.question: kth largest by value (with duplicates) or kth distinct value?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: By value, duplicates counted. For nums = [3,2,3,1,2,4,5,5,6], k=4 the answer is 4 — the multiset, sorted descending, is 6,5,5,4,... so the 4th is 4.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array contain negatives?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, -10⁴ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴. Comparisons handle negatives naturally; no assumptions about sign.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is k guaranteed to be within bounds?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, 1 ≤ k ≤ n, so there's always a valid kth largest — no empty-input handling needed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I mutate the input array?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Worth asking — quickselect reorders nums in place. If the caller needs the original order preserved, copy first or use the heap approach.

examples.explanation: Sorted descending: 6,5,5,4,3,2,2,1. Duplicates count, so the 4th element is 4.
Single element; the 1st largest is itself.

diagrams.title: Choosing the selection strategy
diagrams.caption: Sort is simplest; size-k min-heap wins for streaming/small k; quickselect is O(n) average in place.

approaches.name: Sort and Index
approaches.whenToMention: State first as the obvious baseline, then say 'but the prompt asks if we can do better than sorting'.
hints: If the array were sorted, where would the kth largest sit?
Sort ascending; the kth largest is at index n − k. Sort descending; it's at index k − 1.
It works and is one line, but the problem explicitly nudges 'can you do it without sorting?' — flag the wasted work of fully ordering when you need one element.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Comparison sort dominates at O(n log n). Space is O(1) for an in-place sort or O(n) for a copy; either way more work than needed since we want a single position.
approaches.explanation:
The most direct route: order the whole array, then read off the element at the kth-largest position.

**The index arithmetic.** After sorting **ascending**, the largest element is at index `n−1`, the 2nd largest at `n−2`, and in general the kth largest is at index `n−k`. (Sorting descending instead puts it at `k−1`.) Getting this off-by-one right is the only real trap in this approach — say the formula out loud.

**Why it's correct and why it's wasteful.** Sorting trivially places every element in rank order, so indexing is guaranteed right. But we computed the position of *all* n elements to use exactly *one*. The problem's parenthetical 'Can you solve it without sorting?' is a direct hint that the interviewer wants a selection algorithm, not a full sort.

**When it's actually the right call.** If you'll answer many queries for different k on the same array, sort once (O(n log n)) and answer each query in O(1) — amortised, sorting wins. Mention this; it shows you weigh the workload, not just the single-query cost.

**Why we move on.** For a single query the heap (O(n log k)) and quickselect (O(n) average) both beat O(n log n), and the prompt is fishing for them. Use sort as the baseline you improve upon.
approaches.insight: kth largest = element at index n−k after ascending sort. Nailing that index instantly (and noting sort wins for repeated queries) signals you think about the access pattern, not just the asymptotics.

dryRun.intro: Sort ascending, then index n − k.

java.explanation: Ascending sort; O(n log n) and mutates the input.
kth largest sits at index n − k after ascending sort.

python.explanation: Index n − k is the kth largest.

edgeCases.behavior: Sorted [1,2], index 0 → returns 1 (the smallest, i.e. 2nd largest).

pitfalls: Off-by-one: using n − k + 1 or k − 1 on an ascending sort returns the wrong element.
Mutating the caller's array via in-place sort when order must be preserved.
Ignoring the prompt's hint to avoid sorting — leaves performance on the table.

approaches.name: Min-Heap of Size k
approaches.whenToMention: The clean, safe interview answer — especially for streaming data or when k ≪ n. Code it confidently.
hints: You don't need all elements ranked — only the k largest. What if you maintained just those k as you scan?
Keep a min-heap capped at size k. After pushing each element, if the heap exceeds k, pop the smallest.
After the full scan the heap holds exactly the k largest elements, and its root (the minimum of those) is the kth largest.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of n elements triggers a push and possibly a pop on a heap of size ≤ k, each O(log k) → O(n log k). The heap stores at most k elements → O(k) space. When k ≪ n this is much better than O(n log n).
approaches.explanation:
Instead of ranking everything, keep a running collection of the **k largest elements seen so far** in a **min-heap**.

**Why a min-heap, and why size k.** The kth largest is, by definition, the *smallest* element among the k largest. A min-heap exposes its smallest element at the root in O(1). So if we maintain exactly the k largest values in a min-heap, the root *is* the answer. We enforce 'exactly k' by pushing each scanned element and, whenever the size exceeds k, popping the root — which evicts the smallest of the current candidates. Anything evicted can't be the kth largest because at least k elements are bigger.

**Why min-heap beats the tempting max-heap approach.** A natural first instinct is a max-heap of all n elements, then pop k times. That works but builds a heap of size n (O(n) space) and costs O(n + k log n). The size-k min-heap caps the heap at k, so every operation is O(log k) and space is O(k). When k is small relative to n — the common case — this is dramatically tighter, and it's the version that generalises to *streaming*: you can process an unbounded sequence keeping only k items in memory.

**Why the root is the kth largest after the scan.** At the end, the heap contains the k largest values of the whole array (every larger candidate stayed; everything smaller than all k was evicted). Among those k, the root is the minimum — i.e. the k-th from the top. That's precisely the kth largest overall.

**Duplicates just work.** Equal values occupy separate heap slots and count toward the rank, matching the 'not distinct' requirement: [3,3,3] with k=2 keeps two 3s and returns 3.
approaches.insight: The kth largest is the smallest of the k largest — so a min-heap holding exactly the top k puts the answer at its root. Capping the heap at k (evicting the smallest) is what turns O(n log n) into O(n log k) and makes the method stream-friendly.

dryRun.intro: Min-heap capped at size 2. Push each; if size > 2, pop the smallest. Root at the end is the answer.

java.explanation: Java's default PriorityQueue is a MIN-heap — exactly what we want here.
Cap the heap at k so each op stays O(log k).
Evict the smallest candidate — it can't be among the k largest.
Root = smallest of the k largest = the kth largest.

python.explanation: heapq is a min-heap; push the current value.
Pop the smallest once the heap overflows k.
Index 0 is the min-heap root — the kth largest.

diagrams.title: Size-k min-heap as a sliding 'top-k' filter
diagrams.caption: Each new element pushes in; if the heap overflows k, the smallest is evicted. The root is always the kth largest so far.

edgeCases.behavior: Heap keeps two 3s; root = 3 — duplicates counted correctly.
Heap never overflows; root is the global minimum, which is the nth (smallest) largest.

pitfalls: Using a max-heap and popping k times — O(n) space and slower when k ≪ n.
Forgetting the size cap, letting the heap grow to n (O(n log n), defeats the purpose).
Returning poll() instead of peek() at the end — poll removes the answer; peek reads it.

approaches.name: Quickselect — Partition Toward Index n−k (Optimal Average)
approaches.whenToMention: When asked to beat O(n log k) or for the theoretically fastest average-case in-place solution.
hints: kth largest is the (n − k)th smallest in 0-indexed sorted order. If you could place just *that* index correctly, you'd be done — no full sort.
Partition around a pivot (Lomuto): everything smaller goes left, larger goes right, and the pivot lands at its final sorted position p.
If p == n − k you're done. If p < n − k recurse on the right side; if p > n − k recurse on the left. Randomize the pivot to avoid O(n²) on sorted input.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each partition is O(size). Because we recurse into only ONE side, expected work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … = O(n) on average. A pathological pivot sequence (e.g. always the extreme on sorted input) degrades to n + (n−1) + … = O(n²); random pivots make that astronomically unlikely. O(1) extra space (in place).
approaches.explanation:
Quickselect is quicksort that only ever recurses into the half containing the answer.

**The target index.** Sorting ascending, the kth largest lands at index `target = n − k`. Quickselect's job is to get the element that *belongs* at `target` into `target` — without sorting the rest. We never need the full order, only that one position fixed.

**How one partition step makes progress.** Pick a pivot and run a Lomuto partition: walk the range, pushing every element strictly smaller than the pivot to the left, then swap the pivot into the boundary `store`. Now the pivot sits at its **final sorted index** `p`: everything left of `p` is smaller, everything right is ≥. Three cases follow. If `p == target`, the pivot *is* the answer — return it. If `p < target`, the answer is further right, so recurse (or loop) on `[p+1, right]`. If `p > target`, recurse on `[left, p−1]`. Each step discards one side entirely.

**Why it's O(n) average but O(n²) worst.** Discarding one side means the expected problem size halves each step, so the total work is the geometric series `n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n = O(n)`. The disaster case is a pivot that barely shrinks the range — e.g. always picking the largest element on already-sorted input — giving `n + (n−1) + … = O(n²)`. **Randomizing the pivot** (pick a uniformly random index in `[left, right]`) destroys any adversarial ordering: the chance of repeatedly bad pivots decays exponentially, so worst case is effectively unreachable in practice. This is the single most important implementation detail — without it, sorted input quietly becomes quadratic.

**Why O(1) space and a caveat.** Partitioning is in place with a constant number of pointers; using a loop (not recursion) keeps the stack flat too. The trade-off: quickselect **mutates the input array's order**. If the caller needs the original ordering, copy first — that's the right clarifying question to raise. Duplicates are fine: equal elements distribute around the pivot consistently and the target index still resolves to the correct value.
approaches.insight: Quickselect beats sorting because it throws away half the array each step — it solves a selection problem, not an ordering problem. The whole trick is mapping 'kth largest' to the fixed index n−k and partitioning until a pivot lands exactly there; randomizing the pivot is what keeps the average O(n) honest.

java.line: int target = nums.length - k; // kth largest = (n-k)th smallest
java.explanation: Map the problem to a single 0-indexed position we must fix.
Random pivot — the guard against O(n²) on sorted/adversarial input.
Pivot landed exactly at the target index → nums[p] is the answer.
Answer is to the right; discard the left side entirely.

java.line: swap(nums, store, right); // pivot to its final sorted spot
java.explanation: After this, everything left of store < pivot, so store is the pivot's true rank.

python.line: target = len(nums) - k  # kth largest = (n-k)th smallest
python.explanation: The single index quickselect drives toward.
Randomized pivot to keep the average at O(n).
Pivot in its final position equals the target index → done.
Lomuto: push elements smaller than the pivot to the left boundary.
Drop the parked pivot into its final sorted slot; return that index.

diagrams.title: Quickselect recursion into one side
diagrams.caption: Each partition fixes the pivot's index p, then we keep only the side containing target = n − k.

edgeCases.behavior: left == right immediately → loop body skipped → return nums[0] = 1.
Random pivot prevents O(n²); target = 4 resolves to 5. Deterministic last-pivot would degrade here.
Every element equals the pivot; partition puts all in one block, pivot lands consistently, target index returns 7.

pitfalls: Using a deterministic pivot (first/last element) — O(n²) on sorted input.
Wrong target: kth largest is index n − k, not n − k + 1 or k − 1.
Using `<=` instead of `<` in the partition scan — can mishandle duplicates and infinite-loop the boundary.
Forgetting quickselect mutates the input — clarify whether the caller needs original order.

commonMistakes: Returning the kth distinct value instead of counting duplicates.
Using a max-heap of all n elements instead of a size-k min-heap.
Off-by-one on the quickselect target index (n − k).
Not randomizing the quickselect pivot, causing O(n²) on sorted input.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Max-heap of size n instead of min-heap of size k
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A max-heap of all n elements popped k times costs O(n + k log n) and O(n) space. A size-k min-heap is O(n log k) and O(k) space — tighter when k ≪ n and stream-friendly.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
max_heap = [-x for x in nums]
heapq.heapify(max_heap)        # O(n) space
for _ in range(k - 1):
    heapq.heappop(max_heap)
return -max_heap[0]
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
min_heap = []
for num in nums:
    heapq.heappush(min_heap, num)
    if len(min_heap) > k:      # cap at k
        heapq.heappop(min_heap)
return min_heap[0]

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong quickselect target index
commonMistakesDetailed.why: kth largest equals the (n − k)th smallest in 0-indexed order. Using n − k + 1 or k − 1 selects the wrong element.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int target = nums.length - k + 1; // off by one
// ... partition toward target ...
commonMistakesDetailed.good: int target = nums.length - k;     // kth largest = (n-k)th smallest

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Deterministic pivot on sorted input
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Always picking the last element as pivot makes already-sorted arrays shrink the range by 1 each step → O(n²). A random pivot keeps the average at O(n).
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: pivot_index = right  # last element -- O(n^2) on sorted input

followupVariations.hint: Count frequencies, then size-k heap or quickselect/bucket-sort on counts — same selection idea on frequencies.

followupVariations.hint: Select k smallest by squared distance — size-k max-heap or quickselect on the distance metric.

followupVariations.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
followupVariations.hint: The streaming version — a persistent size-k min-heap answers each add() in O(log k).

patternNote: Selection without full sorting. A size-k min-heap (O(n log k)) holds the top-k with the answer at its root and shines for streams; quickselect (O(n) average) partitions toward index n − k in place. Recognise both whenever you need the kth largest/smallest or top-k. Same family as Top K Frequent Elements, K Closest Points, and Kth Largest in a Stream.
